item.title: Lifted surgery: Fast processing with QLDPC codes
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Lifted surgery executes fast, parallel, and addressable logical Pauli measurements on Abelian group algebra QLDPC codes in a single syndrome extraction round. For a $[[90, 8, 10]]$ radial code, it matches the logical performance of standard code surgery while using 10 times fewer syndrome measurement rounds.

Grade 0.521 · 2.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Lucas Berent, Lawrence Z. Cohen, Armanda O. Quintavalle

Figure

Logical block error rate as a function of physical circuit-level error rate p for single-round scalar lifted surgery operations across different QLDPC codes.

Asks

How can fast, low-time-overhead code surgery be constructed for general Abelian group algebra QLDPC codes without large spatial overheads?

Before

Standard code surgery incurs repeated syndrome extraction rounds scaling with distance d, while existing fast surgery approaches require large auxiliary qubit overheads or specialize only to hypergraph product codes.

But

Restricted to CSS-type (purely Z- or purely X-type) logical Pauli measurements; benchmarked via numerical circuit-level depolarizing noise simulations.

Tools

Abelian group algebra block decomposition · Koszul complexes · integer linear programming circuit scheduling · detector sparsification with correlated decoding

Abstract

Quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes are a leading candidate for achieving low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computing. However, the time overhead of logical operations in QLDPC codes remains a key challenge. Code surgery, a space-efficient technique for fault-tolerant logical measurements, incurs this overhead through repeated rounds of syndrome measurement. We introduce lifted surgery, a method for fast and parallel surgery on Abelian group algebra codes that maintains the low physical overhead that makes QLDPC codes attractive. Lifted surgery preserves the symmetries of the underlying code, making searches for large instances tractable and offering a natural route towards efficient hardware implementations. We utilise block decompositions and techniques from commutative algebra to characterise lifted surgery, investigate well-behaved subfamilies, and construct explicit examples. In particular, we present quantum radial codes with parameters $[[90, 8, 10]]$ and $[[198, 8, 16 ]]$ for which surgery is fast, parallel, and addressable, allowing arbitrary sets of independent logical operators of the same Pauli type to be measured in a single round of syndrome extraction. We benchmark lifted surgery under circuit-level depolarising noise and, for the $[[ 90, 8, 10 ]]$ code, find logical performance comparable to standard code surgery while requiring ten times fewer rounds of syndrome measurement. By combining speed and parallelism, lifted surgery offers a practical route towards low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum computing.

item.title: Local decoders for fault-tolerant quantum computation and translation-invariant stabilizer codes
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Every translation-invariant topological Pauli stabilizer code is locally decodable under phenomenological noise with a non-zero threshold, and a 2D fault-tolerant quantum computer can operate using strictly local operations and constant quantum and classical resource density.

Grade 0.504 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery” · Nathaniel Selub, Aditya Bhardwaj, Ethan Lake

Figure

Schematic of the 2D local fault-tolerant quantum architecture, showing a 1D array of folded surface-code patches decoded on-chip by constant-density classical cellular automata alongside a local 2D classical program-control computer.

Asks

Can scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation based on topological codes in fewer than four dimensions be implemented using strictly local operations, bounded communication speeds, and constant resource density?

Before

All prior local decoders for two-dimensional topological codes required per-site classical resources scaling at least polylogarithmically with system size, and prior fault-tolerant architectures in <4 spatial dimensions required non-local classical computation or communication.

But

Classical computation and communication components are assumed to be noiseless; phenomenological noise assumes p-bounded Pauli and bit-flip errors on data qubits and syndrome measurements.

Tools

cellular-automaton (CA) decoder · spacetime multiscale clustering · folded surface code · lattice surgery · hierarchical slice architecture

Abstract

We construct the first fully spatially local fault-tolerant quantum computer based on topological codes in fewer than four spatial dimensions. Our construction is a two-dimensional architecture that uses only geometrically local quantum and classical operations, bounded-speed classical communication and computation, and a constant density of quantum and classical resources. The core component is a new time-translation-invariant cellular-automaton decoder for the surface code. This decoder preserves logical information for a time stretched-exponential in the code distance and operates continuously during state injection, stabilizer-state preparation, lattice surgery, and transversal readout. We also prove that every translation-invariant topological Pauli stabilizer code is locally decodable under phenomenological noise.

item.title: Demonstration of a logical Bell-state measurement beyond the linear-optical limit
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Realised linear-optical logical Bell-state measurement using a two-qubit repetition code, reaching a mean success probability of (70.8±0.4)% and an average measurement discrimination fidelity of (91.7±0.5)%.

Grade 0.488 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “High-threshold and low-overhead fault-tolerant quantum memory” · Shreya Kumar, Simon D. Reiß, Peter van Loock, Stefanie Barz

Figure

Measured versus theoretical click-pattern probability distributions for the four logical Bell states, showing ambiguous and unambiguous outcomes yielding (70.8±0.4)% mean success probability.

Asks

Can quantum error-correcting codes be used to experimentally demonstrate a logical Bell-state measurement with a success probability exceeding the linear-optical limit without ancillary photons?

Before

Standard static linear-optical Bell-state measurements on dual-rail qubits without ancillary photons are fundamentally limited to a maximum success probability of 50%.

But

Post-selected on four-fold coincidences with background subtraction; repetition code only detects single bit flips rather than providing full error correction.

Tools

Two-qubit repetition code / QPC(1,2) · Type-II ppKTP Sagnac SPDC sources · Fibre-based balanced beam splitters and PBSs · Pseudo-photon-number-resolving detection · Post-selection on four-fold coincidences

Abstract

Fault tolerance is essential for scalable quantum technologies and is enabled by quantum error-correction codes. Bell-state measurements (BSMs) are a fundamental building block for modern quantum technologies such as measurement-based quantum computation and fusion-based quantum computation, as well as quantum networks. Therefore, performing BSMs on error-corrected qubits is a necessary step for achieving fault tolerance in these applications. In this work, we realise a logical BSM using linear optics, based on a two-qubit repetition code, an instance of a quantum parity code that allows detection of bit-flip errors, and experimentally achieve a mean success probability of (70.8 +/- 0.4)%. While standard linear-optical BSMs are fundamentally limited to a maximum success probability of 50%, this increased success probability enables higher secure key rates in quantum communication and facilitates the generation of large graph states for quantum computation. Since fault-tolerant schemes require error-correction codes regardless, this improvement comes at no additional resource overhead. Our results demonstrate that error-correction codes can be used to surpass the linear-optics limit of BSMs, which is an important step towards practical, fault-tolerant, and scalable photonic quantum technologies.

item.title: Low-cost algorithm-to-execution framework for surface-code quantum computing
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Unified algorithm-to-execution framework reduces fault-tolerant space-time volume up to 241.5× via non-Clifford supply co-design and cuts routed latency across twenty benchmark circuits.

Grade 0.463 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “resource estimation: physical qubit and runtime budgets for useful algorithms” · Yunxin Tang, Zixuan Huo, Junxiang Huang, Zhou You, Zhirao Wang, Zhenai Ding, Yumeng Zeng, Yangyu Lu, Yiming Huang, Zongkang Zhang, Haipeng Xie, Ying Li, Jinzhao Sun, Xiao Yuan, Yuan Yao

Figure

Space-time volume and latency variations across twenty benchmark circuits comparing standard baseline layouts and synthesis against circuit-specific layouts and optimized non-Clifford allocations.

Asks

How can circuit scheduling, spatial patch layout, and non-Clifford resource supply be coordinated to minimize physical execution overhead in surface-code quantum computing?

But

Modeled on surface-code simulations with fixed physical error rate pphys=10−3 or 10−4 and 500 ns stabilizer rounds; excludes repetitions for algorithmic success probability.

Tools

surface code lattice surgery · executable workload extraction · direct-rotation state preparation · magic state distillation and cultivation

Abstract

The execution of useful quantum algorithms on fault-tolerant processors requires more than a mapping from logical gates to encoded operations: the spatial organization, non-Clifford resource supply, and execution schedule must also be determined while keeping physical overhead within practical limits. Although the theoretical hierarchy from logical circuits to fault-tolerant operations is well established, these implementation choices are often specified and optimized separately. Here we develop a low-cost algorithm-to-execution framework for surface-code quantum computing. From hierarchical algorithm descriptions, it constructs dependency-preserving logical schedules and an executable workload capturing logical interactions, operation parallelism, and time-resolved non-Clifford demand, thereby linking logical computation to surface-code organization, resource-state preparation, and fault-tolerant execution in a traceable workflow. We apply the framework to twenty benchmark circuits across seven algorithm families and a hierarchically composed application-scale elliptic-curve discrete-logarithm workload. Physical costs vary substantially even for circuits with similar logical resource counts. Under our direct-rotation calibration, non-Clifford implementation selection reduces space-time volume by up to 241.5 times versus an all-synthesis baseline for the QAOA amplitude-amplification workload. Circuit-specific surface-code layouts reduce routed-latency estimates for all twenty benchmarks; thirteen also reduce space-time volume because communication savings outweigh added spatial overhead. These results show that low-cost fault-tolerant execution depends on computation scheduling and organization, not aggregate logical resource counts alone.

item.title: Walking Floquet code circuits for zero-overhead leakage reduction
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Two zero-overhead walking honeycomb Floquet code circuits remove leakage periodically while maintaining code distance to Pauli errors. They correct as many leakage errors as Pauli errors for two noise models and outperform the same-distance walking surface code in the finite-error-rate waterfall regime.

Grade 0.454 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold” · Hanna Westerheim, Kaavya Sahay, Shruti Puri

Figure

Logical error rate versus physical error rate across code distances for swirling and sliding honeycomb Floquet codes compared against the walking surface code under four leakage noise models.

Asks

Can leakage reduction units be integrated into honeycomb Floquet code syndrome extraction circuits with zero gate and depth overhead while preserving code distance?

But

Simulated on toric honeycomb lattices with periodic boundary conditions using minimum-weight perfect matching decoders, uniform leakage probability p, and idealized Clifford/leakage channels.

Tools

swirling and sliding honeycomb Floquet code circuits · zero-overhead SWAP compilation · two-body check measurements · Monte Carlo circuit simulation

Abstract

Leakage, occurring when a qubit undetectably exits the computational subspace, poses a significant challenge for quantum error correction by inducing correlated errors in space and time. These correlations reduce both the code threshold and the effective code distance. To address this challenge, we introduce two zero-overhead walking circuits for the honeycomb Floquet code (hFC), termed the swirling and sliding circuits, which periodically remove leakage while dynamically protecting logical qubits via a schedule of anticommuting two-body measurements. Unlike previous dynamic circuits for the hFC, ours preserves the distance to Pauli errors. We further study their performance under leakage and find that, for two leakage noise models, they may correct as many leakage errors as Pauli errors, improving on the more widely known walking surface code. Through numerical simulation, we observe that finite-error-rate performance under leakage is strongly influenced by entropic effects, producing a pronounced waterfall regime in which the logical error rate decreases much more rapidly with physical error rate than the expected distance-limited scaling. In this regime, even when asymptotic predictions suggest otherwise, the hFC can outperform the same-distance walking surface code in error rates and sub-threshold logical error scaling.

item.title: The generalised semi-Clifford conjecture is false
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Zeng–Chen–Chuang generalised semi-Clifford conjecture is false: an explicit five-qubit gate in 𝒞5∖𝒞4 is not generalised semi-Clifford, and its inverse lies outside the entire Clifford hierarchy.

Grade 0.421 · 1.5σ above the day's baseline · matched “Fault-tolerant quantum computation by anyons” · Nadish de Silva, Oscar Lautsch

Figure

Five-qubit quantum circuit counterexample composed of two-control multiplexed Clifford operations: ctrl𝚍⁡(A) followed by ctrl𝚌⁡(B).

Asks

Are all quantum gates in the Clifford hierarchy generalised semi-Clifford gates of the form C1ΠDC2?

Before

Held for all third-level gates 𝒞3 for arbitrarily many qubits (Beigi–Shor 2008).

But

Counterexample constructed at five qubits (n=5) and level k=5; extends to all n≥5 and k≥5 via identity tensors.

Tools

multiplexed-Clifford gate ansatz · symplectic linear algebra · Lagrangian subspaces over Z₂ · Pauli commutation constraints

Abstract

The Clifford hierarchy is a nested sequence of sets of quantum gates that can be fault-tolerantly performed using gate teleportation within standard quantum error correction schemes. The importance of these gates has motivated numerous studies of their structure. Zeng-Chen-Chuang conjectured in 2007 that all hierarchy gates are generalised semi-Clifford, i.e. take the form C₁ ΠD C₂ for Clifford gates C₁, C₂, a permutation gate Π, and a diagonal gate D; Beigi-Shor proved in 2008 that this holds for all third-level gates. We construct a five-qubit gate that is in the fifth level of the Clifford hierarchy but is not generalised semi-Clifford. Rather than simply present and verify our counterexample to the generalised semi-Clifford conjecture, we show how its form can be deduced. Our counterexample also demonstrates that the Clifford hierarchy is not closed under inverses.
